description.value: The study examined relationships between baseline and longitudinal brain volumetric measures and total alcohol consumed between baseline and six-month follow-up in alcohol-dependent patients.
The study included a cross-sectional baseline investigation and a longitudinal six-month follow-up investigation in alcohol-dependent patients, with healthy subjects assessed at baseline.

spans.text: All participants (patients and controls) underwent a high-resolution volumetric T1-weighted MRI scan (1.5T Signa Advance Echospeed; General Electric Milwaukee, WI) which consisted of a set of 128 adjacent axial planes parallel to the anterior commissure–posterior commissure line with a pixel size of 0.9375 mm 2 and slice thickness of 1.5 mm, using a spoiled gradient echo sequence (repetition time = 10.3 ms; echo time = 2.1 ms; field of view = 240 × 180 mm 2 ; matrix = 256 × 192).
Only 11 of the 19 patients consented for a follow-up examination 6 months after the first one.

The more compromised these WM regions, particularly frontal association areas involved in executive functions and behavioral regulation, the more likely recently detoxified alcohol-dependent patients were to have difficulty abstaining from alcohol consumption.

This indicated that limited alcohol consumption correlated with increased GM volumes in those regions. There were no positive correlations between GM volumetric changes and interim drinking.

value: Regression analysis between the total amount of alcohol consumed between baseline and follow-up and WM changes yielded significant negative correlations in the body and splenium of the corpus callosum and the superior corona radiata. These findings reflect improvement with reduction of alcohol consumption or further degradation with resumption of heavy alcohol consumption in interhemispheric connectivity and connectivity within the limbic system.
